excerpt.en: My first instinct is always the connection between things, not the things themselves — even when nobody else sees the thread. What that costs, and what it's worth.
excerpt.de: Mein erster Instinkt ist immer die Verbindung zwischen den Dingen, nicht die Dinge selbst — auch wenn niemand sonst den Faden sieht. Was das kostet und was es wert ist.

body.en:
Ask me what I noticed about a thing and I'll almost never start with the thing. I'll start with what it's connected to — the dependency two steps upstream, the incentive that shaped it, the pattern it rhymes with somewhere unrelated.

This is my default mode, not a technique I switch on. And I've learned it's not universal: the connections that feel loud and obvious to me are often invisible, or "insignificant," to other people in the room.

## What it's good for

- Seeing second-order effects before they arrive.
- Diagnosing the *actual* cause instead of the loudest symptom.
- Transferring a solution from one domain into another that looks nothing alike.

## What it costs

- I can over-connect — treating a coincidence as a system.
- Explaining the thread takes longer than anyone wants to listen.
- "Obvious to me" is a trap; the burden is on me to make it legible.

## The real work

The skill isn't seeing connections. It's *filtering* them, then translating the ones that matter into something a non-systems-thinker can act on.

## Notes to self

- Concrete story where a connection I saw early paid off (or embarrassingly didn't).
- Tie to the "concepts, not facts" post — same underlying wiring.
